` (459-484). 29 30 **Dead props.** `organizations` (61) and `patientId` (62) declared but never used (destructuring at 91-99 omits them); the V2 adapter still passes `patientId` (definitions/encounter.tsx:23). 31 32 **V2 definition** `src/components/QuestionnaireV2/structured/definitions/encounter.tsx`: requires `["encounterId","facilityId"]` (35), subjects `["encounter"]` (36), validate delegates on `encounters[0]` (38-39), buildRequests → `PUT /api/v1/encounter/{encounterId}/` per entry with a cherry-picked body (48-61). 33 34 ## ChargeItemQuestion (343) — `src/components/Questionnaire/QuestionTypes/ChargeItemQuestion.tsx` 35 36 **State model.** Local-only: `useState` of `ApplyChargeItemDefinitionRequestWithObject[]` (207-209) — a widened type carrying display objects `charge_item_definition_object` / `performer_actor_object` (69-72). The component **never reads** `questionnaireResponse.values`; the response is write-only, so a draft/resume can never rehydrate rows. Display objects are stripped by an identical `.map` destructure repeated three times before every response write (223-229, 249-255, 272-278). 37 38 **Seeding.** None (no server fetch, no response read). Add flow: selecting in `ResourceDefinitionCategoryPicker` sets `selectedChargeItemDefinition`; a `useEffect` (211-244) appends a row (`quantity: "1"`, `encounter: encounterId`, 213-218), writes the response, resets selection. The effect lists `updateQuestionnaireResponseCB` in its dep array (238-244) — the loop hazard adapt.ts:8-9 memoizes against. 39 40 **Value shape.** `{type:"charge_item", value: ApplyChargeItemDefinitionRequest[]}` (231); `quantity` is a **string** (src/types/billing/chargeItem/chargeItem.ts:77-86). 41 42 **Validation.** `CHARGE_ITEM_FIELDS` defines quantity-required (62-67) and `FieldError` renders it per row (116-122), but no validate function is exported and the V2 definition wires none (definitions/chargeItem.tsx:26-45) — quantity errors can only arrive from server error mapping. 43 44 **UI.** Table rows (`ChargeItemForm` 86-194): quantity Input, price popover via `ChargeItemPriceDisplay` (146-151), `UserSelector` performer (158-170), dropdown remove (173-190); bottom picker queries `chargeItemDefinitionApi.listChargeItemDefinition` status=active (333-337). 45 46 **V2 definition** `definitions/chargeItem.tsx`: requires `["encounterId","facilityId"]` (29), subjects `["encounter"]` (30), buildRequests → one `POST .../charge_item/apply_charge_item_defs/` with `{requests: chargeItems}` (32-44). 47 48 ## AppointmentQuestion (293) — `src/components/Questionnaire/QuestionTypes/AppointmentQuestion.tsx` 49 50 **State model.** Most fragmented of the five: response holds `CreateAppointmentQuestion[]` (137-140, single entry defaulted to `{tags:[], note:""}` at 140), plus five local `useState`s — `selectedResource` (112-115), sheet `open` (132), `selectedDate` (134), `selectedSlotId` (135), `selectedSlot` details (164) — plus a **global localStorage-persisted jotai atom** `scheduleServiceTypeAtom` (109-111; `atomWithStorage` in src/atoms/scheduleServiceTypeAtom.ts:12-15) caching last resource type across sessions/logouts, with a resync effect (117-123). 51 52 **Seeding.** From the atom + current user: `getInitialResourceState` (76-97) defaults Practitioner-type resource to the logged-in user. No server seeding of the response value. 53 54 **Value shape.** `CreateAppointmentQuestion {note, slot_id, tags: string[]}` (src/types/scheduling/schedule.ts:277-281). Tag ids resolved to objects for display via `useTagConfigs` per-id query fan-out (175-178). 55 56 **Type-specific logic.** `handleUpdate` (142-161) clears the response to `[]` when note/slot_id/tags are all empty (144-153), else writes the single entry (155-159). Validator `validateAppointmentQuestion` (63-74): slot_id required only when the question is required. 57 58 **UI.** Reuses BookAppointment page components wholesale: `AppointmentFormSection` (182-192), `AppointmentDateSelection` + `AppointmentSlotPicker` inside a Sheet (207-288); error ring on slot via `useFieldError` (133, 199-206). 59 60 **V2 definition** `definitions/appointment.tsx`: requires `["facilityId"]` (31), subjects `["patient","encounter"]` (32), validate on `appointments[0]` with required flag (34-35), buildRequests → `POST /slots/{slot_id}/create_appointment/` body `{note, patient, tags}` guarded on `patientId` (43-56). 61 62 ## FileQuestion (195) — `src/components/Questionnaire/QuestionTypes/FileQuestion.tsx` 63 64 **State model.** Dual source of truth: `useFileUpload` hook owns the `File` objects (123-129), the response owns `FileUploadQuestion[]` (104-105). The registry is a total record over all 11 types (structured/registry.ts:42-54). 90 91 Exceptions/notes: 92 - `MedicationRequestQuestion` has a second consumer: `buildMedicationForTemplate` imported by `src/components/Questionnaire/ManageResponseTemplatesSheet.tsx:87`; that sheet itself is imported only by ServiceRequestQuestion.tsx and MedicationRequestQuestion.tsx — alive solely through adapted legacy components. 93 - **`FieldError.tsx` (33 lines)**: imported only by ServiceRequestQuestion.tsx:10, ChargeItemQuestion.tsx:30, MedicationRequestQuestion.tsx:66. V2 has zero imports of it — alive only transitively. 94 - The legacy fill stack (QuestionnaireForm + `components/Questionnaire/structured/` handlers) is deleted; types.ts:29-31 records that the legacy structured map "went with the legacy fill stack that was its only consumer", and `grep "QuestionnaireForm"` hits only QuestionnaireV2 files. 95 96 **Other `src/components/Questionnaire/` survivors and who reaches them:** 97 - Legacy-only (alive via adapted QuestionTypes): `AddToTemplateDialog` (← MedicationRequest/ServiceRequest), `MedicationValueSetSelect` (← MedicationRequestQuestion), `EntitySelectionDrawer` (← Allergy/Diagnosis/Symptom/MedicationStatement/MedicationRequest), `ManageResponseTemplatesSheet`, `ValueSetSearchContent` (← MedicationValueSetSelect + ValueSetSelect). 98 - Shared with V2 and beyond: `QuestionnaireSearch` (← QuestionnaireV2/fill/QuestionnaireFillPage.tsx + pages/Encounters/tabs/responses.tsx), `OrgSelector` (← QuestionnaireV2/manage/OrganizationsField.tsx), `SelectOrCreateValueset` (← QuestionnaireV2/builder/AnswerOptionsEditor.tsx), `ValueSetSelect` (← 6 legacy QuestionTypes + V2 studio/builder/engine inputs + ~10 non-questionnaire pages), `Questionnaire/data` (← types/questionnaire/structured.ts, V2 fill page, V2 builder QuestionTypePicker, 2 legacy QuestionTypes). 99 100 ## Shared helpers the QuestionTypes pull in, and V2's relationship to them 101 102 - `src/types/questionnaire/validation.ts` — `FieldDefinitions` (15-17), `useFieldError` (25-49), `validateFields` (51-115). Consumers: AppointmentQuestion, EncounterQuestion, FileQuestion, MedicationRequestQuestion, MedicationStatementQuestion (grep). **V2 has zero direct imports** of `useFieldError`/`validateFields` — it reaches them only through the legacy components and their exported validators. 103 - `QuestionValidationError` (src/types/questionnaire/batch) is the error currency for both stacks (legacy props; V2 types.ts:3, StructuredSlot errors prop). 104 - `ResponseValue` in `src/types/questionnaire/form.ts:24-36` still hard-codes every structured variant as a union arm (e.g. `RV<"encounter", EncounterEdit[]>` at 36) — the legacy type spine V2 builds on (types.ts:4-7). 105 - V2's primitive inputs are its own (`src/components/QuestionnaireV2/form/engine/inputs/`: Boolean/Choice/Date/DateTimeQuestionInput/Number/Quantity/Text/Time), so `Common/DateTimeInput` (DeathQuestion) and `useFileUpload`/`FileUploadDropdown` (FileQuestion.tsx:10-12, hooks/useFileUpload) are used inside questionnaire code only by the legacy components — V2 has no direct use of either (grep). 106

content.thinking:
I've finished reviewing all five reports and can see the full landscape now. There are 11 core structured types where the V2 adapters are relatively thin wrappers around much larger legacy QuestionTypes, and about two-thirds of the big-six's code is duplicated list-editor logic handling row operations and data prefetching.

The critical architectural issue is that prefetched server rows and user edits are both stored in the same `values[0].value` field, which cascades into multiple P1 bugs—forcing re-upserts, excluding structured types from drafts, and creating race conditions where refetches overwrite unsaved changes. Since Bodhish requires all structured types to support drafts, the redesign needs to cleanly separate the baseline data from user intent. The value shape uses a `ResponseValue` union that hard-codes each type's row structure, with `StructuredDataMap` handling the type-to-row mapping. The slot machinery and registry system are solid and worth keeping, though they need some boundary and slug fixes, and I need to hard-block the type-change hazard. Test coverage has significant gaps—medication_statement, files, appointment, and time_of_death have no functional tests.

There's also no backend fixture with structured questions, so specs rely on frontend pseudo-questionnaire routes with fixed forms. The actions layer needs a generic plugin fill capability rather than Scribe-specific logic. Before proposing solutions, I need to clarify whether we're keeping the current UX (tables, cards, drawers as-is) or redesigning the interaction pattern—that choice fundamentally affects scope and test strategy.

I should also confirm the phasing approach for the six major editors like MedicationRequest, which is already 2,386 lines with dosage sub-models and templates. Does he want all eleven rebuilt in one wave or phased across multiple PRs, and should that be a single mega-PR or stacked sequence?

For the legacy QuestionTypes and their supporting machinery, since nothing reaches them except through adapters after the rebuild, I can safely delete them as part of the cleanup without needing to ask. The template subsystem for MedicationRequest and ServiceRequest should stay but get unified across the forked copies. On the actions rebuild, I need to understand what specifically felt too custom for Scribe about the current `useFillActions` registration pattern. The plugin contract shape is a design choice I should flag—whether to create a generic form-fill provider slot or keep the action registry at the plugin level. For files in drafts, since they can't serialize to localStorage, I'm leaning toward storing just metadata with a re-attach prompt on restore rather than adding IndexedDB complexity, but that's another decision point for him since he wants all structured data to support drafts. The UI parity question is really about scope, so I'll keep that as text.

Now I'm thinking through what the target architecture should look like. The key move is separating baseline data (fetched from the server, immutable in drafts) from user edits, so drafts only persist the changes and can re-fetch the baseline on restore. Rows need stable client IDs to fix the index-keying problem. I'd build a shared list-editor framework—one generic component handling row CRUD, add flows, field rendering via descriptors, notes, status selects, soft-delete flags, and duplicate guards—configured per type with field definitions and edit components.

The type definitions become self-contained modules under `structured/types/` with a contract, type-specific field components, and a model layer that handles row conversion, diffing against baseline, and building requests. The slot machinery mostly stays intact, though P1-13 blocks validation changes and P2-7/P2-8 get fixed. The submit path becomes cleaner: `buildRequests` takes both edits and baseline, submits only dirty rows, which structurally solves P1-14. The draft layer simplifies—draftPolicy goes away since everything serializes, partition logic gets cleaner, and dirty state is now any user edit including structured changes (solving P1-3). Files get special handling.

Now I'm weighing two approaches: a generic config-driven framework that rebuilds all 11 types but risks over-abstraction (the framework trap where something like MedicationRequest's dosage model doesn't fit a generic grid), versus a shared-primitives approach that provides composable hooks and layout components without the config DSL—each type stays readable at 150-400 lines, duplication mostly eliminated, and it avoids the abstraction pitfall.

I'm leaning toward option B. I still have a few clarifying questions to ask—mostly around UI parity, PR structure, and how the actions should be shaped—so I'll batch those together in one question rather than asking them one at a time.

Given Bodhish's terse style and how richly he answered multiple-choice questions before, I think presenting 4 related options at once will work better than the typical one-at-a-time approach. After I get those answers, I'll lay out the full trade-offs for each approach as text so he can see the design implications clearly and decide which direction makes sense.

Let me think through which questions actually matter for the design—UI parity versus a full redesign is the big one that shapes everything else.  Whether files live in drafts or elsewhere is another key decision, especially since it's an exception to his "all structured support draft" rule. Then there's the actions capability question: what "not custom to scribe" really means in practice, who uses it, and whether the Scribe UI gets mounted by the plugin or if we need a generic assistant slot. The PR and branch structure question is less critical—I could fold that into the approach discussion instead of asking it separately, since he's comfortable with git stacks and I can just present the delivery options alongside the design approaches.

Actually, this branch is already PR #16627 waiting for review changes, so the real question is whether we extend that existing PR or open new stacked ones. That's worth clarifying upfront since it affects how we structure the work. Let me mark task #1 as complete and #2 as in progress, then prepare the next round of questions for him.
I've finished exploring and have the full picture, so I'm marking task #1 complete and moving on to ask the remaining architecture-shaping questions.

So we've settled on four key decisions: keeping the UI normalized with a familiar row-editor pattern, excluding files in drafts as the only exception to structured-draftable content, using a generic assistant slot scoped to the session where Scribe will be the first consumer, and bundling everything into the existing PR. Clarifying questions are wrapped up, and now I'm moving into the visual companion work.

For the architectural approach, I'm weighing two main strategies. The first is a config-driven framework where a single generic component gets driven by per-type configuration objects—this maximizes deduplication and makes adding new types cheap, but it tends to collapse under the weight of exceptions like MedicationRequest's nested dosage instructions or Encounter's singleton-edit shape, and the config DSL inevitably grows escape hatches until it's worse than just writing components. The second approach, which I'm leaning toward, is building a composable primitives kit with a small set of tightly-scoped shared pieces that give teams the building blocks without forcing everything into one framework.

The primitives would include a state hook that manages baseline versus edits, stable row IDs, CRUD with soft-delete support, and a merge strategy for seeding from prefetch queries without overwriting in-flight edits. Layout primitives handle the responsive table-to-card shell, mobile collapsible rows, add-entity controls, and unified error display. Each type becomes its own real component—150 to 400 lines—that composes these primitives with its own domain logic, and the definition module colocates the component, model, converter, and validation. This kills the duplication without a DSL, keeps each type readable in isolation, and lets bigger types like MedicationRequest use the primitives where they fit and custom code where they don't. The trade-off is some per-type wiring remains, but that's acceptable if we enforce discipline through linting and code review to prevent drift.

Approach C would be a strangler pattern—keep the legacy components running, put the new state layer behind adapters, and migrate editors one type at a time in later waves. That's the lowest single-step risk, but it conflicts with rearchitecting now and carries the full weight of the old code plus adapter complexity before things simplify. Draft support also stays blocked until each type migrates.

I'm recommending B. Beyond the editor axis, the design has other components that follow from decisions already made—the baseline/edits model, draft simplification, hard-block validation, the assistant slot, fix wave integration, and test strategy. Those go into the design presentation section by section. The skill asks me to propose 2–3 approaches conversationally with a recommendation, then present the design in sections with approval after each. So I'll present A, B, and C and ask which one, then move into the design details.

I'm thinking about how to frame this—conversational prose with reasoning, ending with a question to make the pick unambiguous. That keeps one decision point per message and lets the reasoning carry the weight while the question captures the choice cleanly. content.text:
One structural decision remains before I can write the design: how the rebuilt editors share code. The map data makes the trade-offs concrete, so here are the three viable shapes.

**Approach B — composable primitives kit (my recommendation).** The shared 64% becomes a small set of sharply-bounded primitives, and each type stays a real, readable component that composes them. The core is `useStructuredRows<T>`: it owns baseline-vs-edits separation (server prefetch lands in `baseline`, never in the response values; user intent lives in `edits` with stable client-generated row ids), row CRUD with the entered-in-error soft-delete split, dirty derivation, and duplicate guards. Around it sit layout primitives — a responsive list shell replacing the five hand-rolled table/card dual renders, one add-entity control replacing the five drawer/select forks, one error display replacing the current three — plus unified status selects and notes. Each type's module colocates its component (~150–400 lines of genuinely domain-specific code), its row model with converter and diff-to-requests, and its validator. MedicationRequest keeps custom code where it truly is custom (the dosage-instruction sub-model, product knowledge, prescriptions) while using the primitives everywhere else. This kills the duplication without inventing a config language, and every unit is independently testable.

**Approach A — config-driven framework.** One generic `StructuredListEditor` driven by per-type field/column descriptors; types become mostly-declarative configs. Maximum deduplication and new types get very cheap — but the map shows three types that don't fit a generic list grid (MedicationRequest's nested per-row dosage editor, ServiceRequest's activity-definition-driven row creation, Encounter's singleton edit form). Config DSLs in this situation grow escape hatches until the framework is a new monolith that's harder to debug than the duplication it replaced. I think this is the trap the "zero bugs, maintainability" goal says to avoid.

**Approach C — strangler extraction.** Keep the legacy components, put the new baseline/edits state layer behind the adapters first, migrate editors one at a time in later waves. Lowest risk per step, but it conflicts with "rearchitect them now": the 8.9k legacy lines and their hazards (refetch-clobbers-edits, index-keyed rows) stay alive indefinitely, the adapters get more complex before anything gets simpler, and structured draft support stays blocked until each type migrates.

Regardless of choice, the rest of the design is already fixed by your rulings: baseline/edits separation feeds drafts (P1-3, P1-14 solved structurally), hard-block for broken required slots (P1-13), the assistant slot replaces the action registry, and the fix wave + Playwright expansion ride along.

content.text:
Here's the design, section 1 of 5. This is the load-bearing one — everything else follows from it.

## Section 1 — The state model (why bugs disappear structurally)

Today one array does three jobs: it holds prefetched server rows, user edits, and the submit payload all at once. Every major finding traces back to that conflation — P1-14 (untouched rows re-upsert and clobber another clinician's edit), P1-3 (structured edits can't be draft-tracked because you can't tell a user keystroke from a mount-effect prefetch), the refetch-clobbers-edits race in all five prefetching components, and the blanket `draftPolicy: "exclude"`.

The rebuild splits it in three:

**Baseline** is what the server had. It's owned by the query layer, never written into the response. Prefetch landing no longer mutates form state, so a background refetch can't destroy typed edits and can't manufacture a phantom draft.

**Edits** are user intent, and only user intent: `{ rowId, op: "add" | "update" | "remove", patch }` keyed by a stable client-generated `rowId`. This is what persists to drafts — small, JSON-safe, and meaningful without the server rows, which fixes P1-3 and makes every structured type draftable per your ruling. ## Section 3 — Contract and data flow: response, drafts, submit, validation

**Where edits live.** `QuestionnaireResponse` gains one field: `edits` — the typed edit log. `values[0].value` still carries the projected rows, maintained mechanically by the state core, so everything that reads "the answer" today keeps working untouched: the answered predicate, outline ticks, readonly/preview rendering, and the server-draft `response_dump`. The rule is directional: **display reads projection; persistence and submission read only edits.**

**Contract v2.** `StructuredTypeDefinition` changes three fields. `buildRequests(data, ctx)` becomes `toRequests(edits, ctx)` — compiled from intent, so an untouched section produces zero requests by construction. `validate` receives both projection and edits — projection answers "is a required section satisfied" (existing baseline rows count, matching today's clinical semantics), edits answer "is what the user changed well-formed". `draftPolicy` survives with exactly one `"exclude"` left: files. `requires`/`subjects` and the slot-state machinery are unchanged.

**Drafts and dirty.** Dirty = plain-answer signature change OR any non-empty edit log — so a structured-only Time of Death entry now arms the navigation prompt and writes a recoverable draft (P1-3). Local drafts persist edit logs, never projections; the `preserveExcludedStructured` carry-over complexity mostly dies with the exclusion policy. On restore, components refetch baseline and overlay edits by `rowId`; an edit whose baseline row vanished server-side is dropped **with a visible notice** — honest conflict handling where today a stale snapshot would silently clobber. Draft snapshots also gain `internal_revision` pinning (P1-7's frontend half), so a draft written against an edited questionnaire is flagged stale instead of restored verbatim.

**Submit.** composeBatch reads edits, gains the `missing_context` guard the triage found missing, preflights the 20-request batch cap with a specific error (P1-10), and puts `form_submission: continueDraftId` in the submit body so the backend's linkage and duplicate guard finally fire (P1-9; the status PUT stays until the backend owns that transition — goes on the backend list). The `exists` operator is fixed to honor `answer:false` and skip the unanswered short-circuit, matching the backend evaluator (P1-12).

**Validation — the hard-block ruling, made precise.** A required structured question whose slot is broken (render failure, subject mismatch, missing context, unknown type) blocks submit with an error naming the section. Additionally, any structured question — required or not — whose edit log is non-empty but whose slot is broken also blocks, because recorded user intent would otherwise be silently dropped. Only a non-required, untouched, broken section is skipped: there is nothing to lose. The registry's "parity requirement" comment gets rewritten to state the new invariant: a slot showing a notice is either submittable-as-skipped or named in a blocking error — never silently dropped.

**Page-level guards in the same flow:** the fill page gates mount on `questionnaire.subject_type` matching the route's subject family (P1-1) and on `encounter.patient.id` matching the URL patient (P1-2), rendering the existing error page on mismatch; and submission freezes the session — `isPending` flows through `FormContext` into every input's disabled state, the remove-form button, and the add-questionnaire picker (P1-4's remaining half).

Look right? Section 4 covers the assistant slot that replaces the action registry, plus the remaining fixes (Studio, search scoping, login drafts, agent coercion) and the backend issues hand-off list.

# Questionnaire V2 — Structured rearchitecture + fix wave

Date: 2026-08-03 · Branch: `bodhi/questionnaire-fill` (PR #16627) · Backend fixtures: `care` @ `bodhi/ENG-737-test-fixtures`
Status: design approved section-by-section by Bodhish (5 sections + 3 amendments). Supersedes the adapted-legacy structured layer.

## 1. Goals and non-goals

**Goals**: long-term maintainability, zero known bugs, extensive Playwright coverage, high-quality code. Concretely: rebuild the 11 structured question editors V2-native on a shared primitives kit; fix every confirmed frontend finding from the PR #16627 review triage; rebuild the plugin-fill (actions) layer as a generic capability; expand the Playwright suite to cover every structured type and every architectural invariant; delete the ~8.9k-line legacy `QuestionTypes` layer and its orphaned satellites.

**Non-goals**: backend product fixes (handed off as a written list — §9); server-side drafts beyond what exists (separate feature); assistant-driven structured edits are IN scope (amendment 2), but a full voice UX is not — this wave ships the capability contract; full fill-page state-machine rewrite (only the scoped lifecycle cleanup in §7).

## 2. Decision log (rulings by Bodhish, 2026-08-03)

| # | Decision |
|---|---|
| D1 | P1-13: **hard block** — a required structured question whose slot is broken blocks submit. Extended by design: any broken slot holding recorded edits also blocks (no silent data loss); only non-required + untouched + broken is skipped. |
| D2 | P1-17: localStorage drafts stay, are user-visible, and **all structured types become draftable** — except **files** (D6). Server drafts remain a separate feature. |
| D3 | P1-20: rebuild the Scribe-custom action registry as a **generic plugin fill capability**. No audit requirement — nothing saves without user action. |
| D4 | Backend: **no product fixes by us**; produce a shareable issues list. Amendment 3: backend **fixtures are in scope** — extend the E2E fixture script on the care PR; no frontend fixture hacks. |
| D5 | UI scope: **normalize, keep familiar** — one consistent row-editor pattern, visually close to today; specs updated where normalization changes details. |
| D6 | Files in drafts: **stay excluded** (raw `File` objects; the only exception to D2). |
| D7 | Plugin fill shape: **generic assistant slot** — session-scoped handle; Scribe becomes the first consumer. |
| D8 | Delivery: **everything lands in PR #16627** as sequenced commits. |
| D9 | Architecture: **Approach B — composable primitives kit** (not a config framework, not a strangler migration). |
| A1 | Amendment: draft restore **merges across questionnaire changes** (revision pin triggers merge + notice, not rejection). |
| A2 | Amendment: the assistant handle **writes everything, including structured rows** (schema-validated); enables voice-based form filling; safe because nothing persists until Save. |
| A3 | Amendment: structured test questionnaires are seeded by the **backend fixture script** (care PR), the honest owner; the frontend is its primary user. |

## 3. State model: baseline / edits / projection

Today one array (`response.values[0].value`) holds prefetched server rows, user edits, and the submit payload at once. That conflation is the root cause of P1-14 (untouched rows re-upsert), P1-3 (structured edits invisible to dirty/draft), the refetch-clobbers-edits race, and the blanket `draftPolicy: "exclude"`.

The rebuild splits three concerns:

- **Baseline** — what the server had. Owned by the query layer (TanStack cache), never written into the response. Prefetch/refetch cannot mutate form state, destroy typed edits, or manufacture phantom drafts.
- **Edits** — user intent only: `{ rowId, op: "add" | "update" | "remove", patch }` with stable client-generated `rowId`s (server id for baseline rows, uuid for adds). This is what drafts persist: small, JSON-safe, meaningful without server rows. Replaces index-based row identity (fixes the Diagnosis sorted-vs-server index mismatch).
- **Projection** — `baseline + edits`, computed for display; `edits` alone compile into requests. Dirtiness is **derived**, never a manually-set flag. `dirty` disappears from `DiagnosisRequest` and `MedicationRequestCreate` as a wire field.

`useStructuredRows<T>` owns: projection, row CRUD including the entered-in-error soft-delete split for rows with server ids, duplicate guards, single-row mode (encounter), and `toRequests()` compilation. Type modules supply converter, differ, schema, and domain UI.

## 4. Primitives kit and type modules

Layout: `QuestionnaireV2/structured/` gains `core/` and `types/`; registry, plugin registry, and `form/StructuredSlot.tsx` stay.

**`structured/core/`** — six primitives, one job each:
- `useStructuredRows<T>` — §3 state core.
- `StructuredList` — responsive shell; column/field definitions declared once per type, rendered as desktop grid row AND mobile collapsible card from the same definition. Deletes the five ~100–140-line mobile-card clones, MedicationRequest's twice-rendered advanced fields, and the hand-synced `grid-cols-[…]`/`max-w-[…]` literals.
- `AddEntityControl` — add flow: inline valueset/entity select (desktop), staged-row drawer (mobile). Replaces the five forks around `EntitySelectionDrawer`.
- `RowStatusSelect` — status/verification/clinical-status family with `isExistingRecord` gating. Replaces four copies.
- `StructuredFieldError` — one error display bound to `QuestionValidationError`. Replaces the three coexisting mechanisms.
- `ResponseTemplates` — the template subsystem (query + 2 mutations + dialog + sheet) as one module; today two drifted ~250-line forks (MedicationRequest, ServiceRequest).

`HistoricalRecordSelector` stays; its four ~110–175-line configs collapse into one config helper.

**`structured/types/<type>/`** — per type: `definition.ts` (registry contract), `model.ts` (row type, server→row converter, edits→requests differ, **zod row schema** for A2), editor component, validator where the domain has rules. Sizes: list types ~150–300 lines of domain code. Type-specific ports and corrections:
- **allergy_intolerance / symptom / diagnosis / medication_statement**: straight ports of domain fields (category+criticality icons; severity+duplicate guard; severity+category+onset ordering as a *display* sort, not a write-back; information-source + effective-period). Diagnosis loses the sorted-array write-back.
- **medication_request**: keeps its genuinely custom ~1,200 lines (dosage-instruction sub-editor incl. dose vs taper, PRN, M-A-N timing; product knowledge; prescription creation + alternate_identifier). Sheds duplicated scaffolding; `DosageDialog` becomes a top-level component; advanced-fields render once.
- **service_request**: activity-definition-driven row creation, pricing, requester tools; dual-state + JSON.stringify sync effect eliminated; gets a working validator (legacy one was shape-mismatched and unwired).
- **encounter**: single-row mode; keeps status-driven period sync + hospitalization rules; drops dead props; `?toDischarge` URL coupling made explicit in the definition.
- **charge_item**: becomes response-backed (today write-only local state — resume/drafts can never rehydrate); display-object widening handled in `model.ts` once, not three inline strips.
- **appointment**: five `useState`s + global atom consolidated; **P1-16 fixed** — no request when `slot_id` is absent, and validate flags a missing slot when any other field is set.
- **files**: port with `draftPolicy: "exclude"` (D6); base64 conversion stays in the differ.
- **time_of_death**: trivial port; becomes draftable (was excluded by blanket policy only).

**Deleted at wave end** (last commit, once nothing imports them): all 11 legacy `QuestionTypes` files (~8,862 lines), `EntitySelectionDrawer`, `AddToTemplateDialog`, `ManageResponseTemplatesSheet`, `MedicationValueSetSelect`, `FieldError.tsx`, `useFieldError`/`validateFields` machinery in `types/questionnaire/validation.ts`. `ValueSetSelect` stays (used by ~10 non-questionnaire pages).

## 5. Contract and data flow

**Response shape.** `QuestionnaireResponse` gains `edits?` (typed edit log). `values[0].value` continues to carry the projection, maintained mechanically by the state core — the answered predicate, outline ticks, readonly/preview renderers, and server-draft `response_dump` keep working unchanged. Rule: **display reads projection; persistence and submission read only edits.**

**`StructuredTypeDefinition` v2.** `buildRequests(data, ctx)` → `toRequests(edits, ctx)`; untouched sections produce zero requests by construction (fixes P1-14 for every type at once). `validate(projection, edits, questionId, required)` — projection answers "is a required section satisfied" (baseline rows count, matching clinical semantics); edits answer "is what changed well-formed". `draftPolicy` survives with files as the only `"exclude"`. `requires`/`subjects` and slot-state machinery unchanged.

**Drafts and dirty.** Dirty = plain-answer signature change OR non-empty edit log (P1-3). Local drafts persist edit logs, never projections; `preserveExcludedStructured` complexity mostly dies. Restore: refetch baseline, overlay edits by `rowId`; an edit whose baseline row vanished is dropped **with a visible notice**. Draft snapshots gain `internal_revision` pinning (P1-7 FE half).

**A1 — merge across questionnaire changes.** Revision mismatch triggers a compatibility-aware merge, not rejection: answers restore where the question id still exists with the same type; choice/quantity restore only if the stored coding/value matches a currently-available option; structured edits overlay per the paragraph above. Everything unrestorable is listed in the restore bar ("N answers couldn't be restored…", with labels). The same merge backs P2-3: mid-session questionnaire updates surface an "updated — reload form" banner whose reload runs this merge.

**Submit.** `composeBatch` reads edits; gains the `missing_context` guard; preflights the 20-request batch cap with a specific error (P1-10); puts `form_submission: continueDraftId` in the submit body so backend linkage + duplicate guard fire (P1-9; status PUT stays until backend owns the transition). `exists` operator honors `answer:false` and skips the unanswered short-circuit, matching the backend (P1-12).

**Validation (D1).** Blocking error naming the section when: (a) required + slot broken (renderFailed / subject_mismatch / missing_context / unknown_type), or (b) any question with non-empty edits + slot broken. Skip only non-required + untouched + broken. The registry "parity requirement" comment is rewritten: a slot showing a notice is either submittable-as-skipped or named in a blocking error — never silently dropped.

**Page guards.** Mount gates: `questionnaire.subject_type` must match the route's subject family (P1-1); `encounter.patient.id` must match the URL patient (P1-2) — existing error page on mismatch. Submit freeze: `isPending` flows through `FormContext` into every input's disabled state, remove-form, and the add-questionnaire picker (P1-4).

## 6. Assistant capability (replaces `src/lib/actions/`)

Delete the global action registry and Scribe-specific mount. Plugin manifests gain a `formAssistant` extension point (same path as `structuredQuestionTypes`), registered under the **configured** plugin slug, not the manifest's self-declared name (P2-8). The fill page renders registered assistants and hands each a **session handle** created per fill session (constructed per mount, passed down — no module-global map; P2-9 gone structurally):

- `listForms()`, `listQuestions(formKey)` — descriptors: id, label, type, enabled state, current-value summary; structured descriptors include the zod row schema and current projection.
- `getValue` / `setValue` — plain types through the coercion choke point: integers reject non-integral input; dates parse strict `YYYY-MM-DD` as local dates with round-trip rollover validation (P1-19).
- `applyStructuredEdit(formKey, questionId, {op, rowId?, patch})` (A2) — same edit-log path as human input; rows validated against the type's schema (unknown fields rejected, enums checked, same date/integer rules).
- `subscribe(listener)` — state-change notifications.

Assistant writes appear immediately as ordinary pending edits — reviewable, revertible; nothing persists until Save (why audit is out, D3). Hard-block validation applies on top. Test bridge: the handle is exposed on `window` behind a test/dev env gate so Playwright can drive it (§10).

## 7. Other fixes riding the wave

- **Studio**: save response no longer resets editor state when edits landed during the PUT (P1-5); question type change clears incompatible fields — `structured_type`, `answer_option`, `answer_value_set`, `unit` (P2-4); valueset-backed choice gets real repeats support (P2-5).
- **Session/auth**: draft clearing moves from login submit to auth-success paths (P1-18); drafts cleared on token-refresh failure + swept at app boot (P1-17 boundary gaps); submit aborts with named forms when a form store is missing or retained snapshots exist (P2-6); `PluginErrorBoundary` gets a reset key (P2-7).
- **Fill lifecycle (scoped P2-11)**: explicit session-phase state (editing → composing → submitting) that the freeze rides on; resume orchestration extracted into a hook. Not a full rewrite.
- **Types**: submit TBody rewritten to the real backend shape (`results`/`values`/`body_site`/`form_submission`); composeBatch entries typed; unused wrong routes deleted (P2-1).
- **Perf (P2-10 worst offenders)**: autosave signature moves inside the debounce window and gets cheap by construction (edit logs are small); Studio full-tree validation deferred (`useDeferredValue`). Scroll-spy offset caching only if profiling shows need.
- **Quantity**: valueset unit picks also write `coding` (P1-11 FE half).
- **Picker facility scoping (P2-2)**: frontend wires a facility prop to `QuestionnaireSearch`, but activation waits on the backend facility-or-instance filter (→ §9 list).

## 8. Backend fixture work (care PR `bodhi/ENG-737-test-fixtures`, A3)

Extend `care/fixtures/scripts/questionnaire_e2e_fixtures.py` (idempotent, slug-keyed, deterministic uuid5 ids — existing pattern):
- Per-type structured questionnaires (`e2e-structured-<type>`, encounter subject) covering all 11 core types; required and optional variants where the test matrix needs them.
- A patient-subject fixture questionnaire (today authored live by `fillPatientSubject.spec.ts` — moves here).
- An unknown-plugin-type fixture (`e2e-structured-unknown`, a namespaced `x_e2e.missing` structured question) for hard-block and unknown-type specs.
- A structured kitchen-sink (several structured + plain questions) for session/draft/merge specs.

## 9. Backend hand-off list (separate doc, not committed; technical wording)

MultipleObjectsReturned 500 on draft create (unscoped slug resolution); quantity `coding=None` 500; optimistic concurrency — 409 on stale `internal_revision` for Studio PUTs and submits; S3 write inside the atomic batch (orphaned objects on rollback); 14 response-API tests missing `auth_context`; facility-or-instance list filter (unblocks P2-2); slug filter on the questionnaire list; server-side ownership of the form-submission status transition. Each with repro, impact, suggested fix.

## 10. Test plan

**Helper fixes**: `getQuestionnaireIdBySlug` paginates (P2-12). Helpers stay `questionBlock`-scoped.

**Per-type matrix** (11 types × ): add · edit · remove (asserting entered-in-error soft-delete for server rows) · validation · draft save→reload→restore · submit + on-page verify. Fills every gap in the coverage table — medication_statement, files, appointment, time_of_death go from zero to complete; encounter gets its first submit test.

**Invariant specs** (pin the architecture):
1. Untouched section ⇒ **zero** upsert requests (network-asserted; P1-14 pin).
2. Prefetch/refetch ⇒ no dirty, no draft, no clobbering of in-progress edits.
3. Structured-only edit ⇒ navigation prompt + restorable draft (P1-3 pin).
4. Draft-merge across a questionnaire edit ⇒ restores what fits, lists what didn't (A1 pin).
5. Revision-drift banner ⇒ reload preserves answers.
6. Submit freeze ⇒ inputs disabled during in-flight submit (slow-route interception).
7. 21-entry batch ⇒ specific error, no network (P1-10 pin).
8. Resume submit body carries `form_submission` (P1-9 pin).
9. `exists:false` enable-when matches backend behavior (P1-12 pin).
10. Failed login leaves drafts intact (P1-18 pin).
11. Hard-block errors name the broken section (via `e2e-structured-unknown`).
12. Subject/patient mount guards render the error page (P1-1/P1-2 pins).

**Assistant specs**: drive the window-exposed handle like a voice assistant — fill plain + structured, assert projection renders, Save submits exactly those edits, schema-violating writes rejected.

**Cadence**: per-commit lint + tsc + targeted specs; full questionnaire suite against the local backend at wave end.

## 11. Delivery (D8)

Sequenced commits on `bodhi/questionnaire-fill`, each green: state core → primitives → type ports in reviewable batches → validation flip + drafts/merge → assistant slot → fix bundle → backend fixtures (care PR) + spec expansion throughout → legacy deletion last. PR #16627 description rewritten at the end (sanitized wording per standing rule). Backend hand-off doc delivered as a file.

## 12. Traceability: finding → resolution

| Finding | Resolution here |
|---|---|
| P1-1, P1-2 | §5 page guards |
| P1-3, P1-14 | §3 state model (structural) |
| P1-4 | §5 submit freeze + §7 lifecycle |
| P1-5, P2-4, P2-5 | §7 Studio |
| P1-7 (FE), A1 | §5 drafts + merge |
| P1-9, P1-10, P1-12 | §5 submit |
| P1-11 (FE) | §7 quantity |
| P1-13 | §5 validation (D1) |
| P1-16 | §4 appointment module |
| P1-17 (FE), P1-18 | §7 session/auth |
| P1-19, P1-20, P2-8, P2-9 | §6 assistant capability |
| P2-1, P2-10 | §7 types/perf |
| P2-2 | §7 + §9 (backend filter) |
| P2-3 | §5 A1 merge/banner |
| P2-6, P2-7 | §7 session |
| P2-11 | §7 lifecycle (scoped) |
| P2-12 | §10 helper fix |
| P1-6, P1-8, P1-15, EXTRA-1, P1-11 (BE), P1-7 (BE) | §9 backend hand-off |

Base directory for this skill: /Users/bodhishthomas/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.1.1/skills/writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Remember
- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in every step — if a step changes code, show the code
- Exact commands with expected output
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

Base directory for this skill: /Users/bodhishthomas/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/6.1.1/skills/subagent-driven-development

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. The only reasons to stop are: BLOCKED status you cannot resolve, ambiguity that genuinely prevents progress, or all tasks complete. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

## When to Use

```dot
digraph when_to_use {
    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Stay in this session?" [shape=diamond];
    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];
    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Stay in this session?" [label="yes"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="yes"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "executing-plans" [label="no - parallel session"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
- Same session (no context switch)
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality), broad review at the end
- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)

## The Process

```dot
digraph process {
    rankdir=TB;

    subgraph cluster_per_task {
        label="Per Task";
        "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Implementer subagent asks questions?" [shape=diamond];
        "Answer questions, provide context" [shape=box];
        "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [shape=box];
        "Write diff file, dispatch task reviewer subagent (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)" [shape=box];
        "Task reviewer reports spec ✅ and quality approved?" [shape=diamond];
        "Dispatch fix subagent for Critical/Important findings" [shape=box];
        "Mark task complete in todo list and progress ledger" [shape=box];
    }

    "Read plan, note context and global constraints, create todos" [shape=box];
    "More tasks remain?" [shape=diamond];
    "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent (../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md)" [shape=box];
    "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch" [shape=box style=filled fillcolor=lightgreen];

    "Read plan, note context and global constraints, create todos" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";
    "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" -> "Implementer subagent asks questions?";
    "Implementer subagent asks questions?" -> "Answer questions, provide context" [label="yes"];
    "Answer questions, provide context" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)";
    "Implementer subagent asks questions?" -> "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" [label="no"];
    "Implementer subagent implements, tests, commits, self-reviews" -> "Write diff file, dispatch task reviewer subagent (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)";
    "Write diff file, dispatch task reviewer subagent (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)" -> "Task reviewer reports spec ✅ and quality approved?";
    "Task reviewer reports spec ✅ and quality approved?" -> "Dispatch fix subagent for Critical/Important findings" [label="no"];
    "Dispatch fix subagent for Critical/Important findings" -> "Write diff file, dispatch task reviewer subagent (./task-reviewer-prompt.md)" [label="re-review"];
    "Task reviewer reports spec ✅ and quality approved?" -> "Mark task complete in todo list and progress ledger" [label="yes"];
    "Mark task complete in todo list and progress ledger" -> "More tasks remain?";
    "More tasks remain?" -> "Dispatch implementer subagent (./implementer-prompt.md)" [label="yes"];
    "More tasks remain?" -> "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent (../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md)" [label="no"];
    "Dispatch final code reviewer subagent (../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md)" -> "Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch";
}
```

## Pre-Flight Plan Review

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

Present everything you find to your human partner as one batched question —
each finding beside the plan text that mandates it, asking which governs —
before execution begins, not one interrupt per discovery mid-plan. If the
scan is clean, proceed without comment. The review loop remains the net for
conflicts that only emerge from implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## Handling Implementer Status

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

## Handling Reviewer ⚠️ Items

The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — send it back to the implementer and re-review.

## Constructing Reviewer Prompts

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. When you fill a reviewer template:

- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `scripts/review-package BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- Dispatch fix subagents for Critical and Important findings. Record Minor
  findings in the progress ledger as you go, and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is the human's decision, like any plan
  contradiction: present the finding and the plan text, ask which governs.
  Do not dismiss the finding because the plan mandates it, and do not
  dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan without asking.
- The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
  `scripts/review-package MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
  branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
  printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
  one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands.
- Every fix dispatch carries the implementer contract: the fix subagent
  re-runs the tests covering its change and reports the results. Name the
  covering test files in the dispatch — a one-line fix does not need the
  whole suite. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm the fix report
  contains the covering tests, the command run, and the output; dispatch
  the re-review once all three are present.
- If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix
  subagent with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
  Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
  session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.

## File Handoffs

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files:

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of requirements. Your dispatch should
  contain: (1) one line on where this task fits in the project; (2) the
  brief path, introduced as "read this first — it is your requirements,
  with the exact values to use verbatim"; (3) interfaces and decisions
  from earlier tasks that the brief cannot know; (4) your resolution of
  any ambiguity you noticed in the brief; (5) the report-file path and
  report contract. Exact values (numbers, magic strings, signatures, test
  cases) appear only in the brief.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- Fix dispatches append their fix report (with test results) to the same
  report file and return a short summary; re-reviews read the updated file.

## Durable Progress

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- At skill start, check for a ledger:
  `cat "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.superpowers/sdd/progress.md"`. Tasks listed there
  as complete are DONE — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task
  not marked complete.
- When a task's review comes back clean, append one line to the ledger in
  the same message as your other bookkeeping:
  `Task N: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the ledger (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

## Prompt Templates

- [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md) - Dispatch implementer subagent
- [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md) - Dispatch task reviewer subagent (spec compliance + code quality)
- Final whole-branch review: use superpowers:requesting-code-review's [code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md)

## Example Workflow

```
You: I'm using Subagent-Driven Development to execute this plan.

[Read plan file once: docs/superpowers/plans/feature-plan.md]
[Create todos for all tasks]

Task 1: Hook installation script

[Run task-brief for Task 1; dispatch implementer with brief + report paths + context]

Implementer: "Before I begin - should the hook be installed at user or system level?"

You: "User level (~/.config/superpowers/hooks/)"

Implementer: "Got it. Implementing now..."
[Later] Implementer:
  - Implemented install-hook command
  - Added tests, 5/5 passing
  - Self-review: Found I missed --force flag, added it
  - Committed

[Run review-package, dispatch task reviewer with the printed path]
Task reviewer: Spec ✅ - all requirements met, nothing extra.
  Strengths: Good test coverage, clean. Issues: None. Task quality: Approved.

[Mark Task 1 complete]

Task 2: Recovery modes

[Run task-brief for Task 2; dispatch implementer with brief + report paths + context]

Implementer: [No questions, proceeds]
Implementer:
  - Added verify/repair modes
  - 8/8 tests passing
  - Self-review: All good
  - Committed

[Run review-package, dispatch task reviewer with the printed path]
Task reviewer: Spec ❌:
  - Missing: Progress reporting (spec says "report every 100 items")
  - Extra: Added --json flag (not requested)
  Issues (Important): Magic number (100)

[Dispatch fix subagent with all findings]
Fixer: Removed --json flag, added progress reporting, extracted PROGRESS_INTERVAL constant

[Task reviewer reviews again]
Task reviewer: Spec ✅. Task quality: Approved.

[Mark Task 2 complete]

...

[After all tasks]
[Dispatch final code-reviewer]
Final reviewer: All requirements met, ready to merge

Done!
```

## Advantages

**vs. Manual execution:**
- Subagents follow TDD naturally
- Fresh context per task (no confusion)
- Parallel-safe (subagents don't interfere)
- Subagent can ask questions (before AND during work)

**vs. Executing Plans:**
- Same session (no handoff)
- Continuous progress (no waiting)
- Review checkpoints automatic

**Efficiency gains:**
- Controller curates exactly what context is needed; bulk artifacts move
  as files, not pasted text
- Subagent gets complete information upfront
- Questions surfaced before work begins (not after)

**Quality gates:**
- Self-review catches issues before handoff
- Task review carries two verdicts: spec compliance and code quality
- Review loops ensure fixes actually work
- Spec compliance prevents over/under-building
- Code quality ensures implementation is well-built

**Cost:**
- More subagent invocations (implementer + reviewer per task)
- Controller does more prep work (extracting all tasks upfront)
- Review loops add iterations
- But catches issues early (cheaper than debugging later)

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Start implementation on main/master branch without explicit user consent
- Skip task review, or accept a report missing either verdict (spec compliance AND task quality are both required)
- Proceed with unfixed issues
- Dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts)
- Make a subagent read the whole plan file (hand it its task brief —
  `scripts/task-brief` — instead)
- Skip scene-setting context (subagent needs to understand where task fits)
- Ignore subagent questions (answer before letting them proceed)
- Accept "close enough" on spec compliance (reviewer found spec issues = not done)
- Skip review loops (reviewer found issues = implementer fixes = review again)
- Let implementer self-review replace actual review (both are needed)
- Tell a reviewer what not to flag, or pre-rate a finding's severity in the
  dispatch prompt ("treat it as Minor at most") — the plan's example code is
  a starting point, not evidence that its weaknesses were chosen
- Dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file — generate it first
  (`scripts/review-package BASE HEAD`) and name the printed path in the
  prompt
- Move to next task while the review has open Critical/Important issues
- Re-dispatch a task the progress ledger already marks complete — check
  the ledger (and `git log`) after any compaction or resume

**If subagent asks questions:**
- Answer clearly and completely
- Provide additional context if needed
- Don't rush them into implementation

**If reviewer finds issues:**
- Implementer (same subagent) fixes them
- Reviewer reviews again
- Repeat until approved
- Don't skip the re-review

**If subagent fails task:**
- Dispatch fix subagent with specific instructions
- Don't try to fix manually (context pollution)

## Integration

**Required workflow skills:**
- **superpowers:using-git-worktrees** - Ensures isolated workspace (creates one or verifies existing)
- **superpowers:writing-plans** - Creates the plan this skill executes
- **superpowers:requesting-code-review** - Code review template for the final whole-branch review
- **superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch** - Complete development after all tasks

**Subagents should use:**
- **superpowers:test-driven-development** - Subagents follow TDD for each task

**Alternative workflow:**
- **superpowers:executing-plans** - Use for parallel session instead of same-session execution

# Implementer Subagent Prompt Template

Use this template when dispatching an implementer subagent.

```
Subagent (general-purpose):
  description: "Implement Task N: [task name]"
  model: [MODEL — REQUIRED: choose per SKILL.md Model Selection; an omitted
         model silently inherits the session's most expensive one]
  prompt: |
    You are implementing Task N: [task name]

    ## Task Description

    Read your task brief first: [BRIEF_FILE]
    It contains the full task text from the plan.

    ## Context

    [Scene-setting: where this fits, dependencies, architectural context]

    ## Before You Begin

    If you have questions about:
    - The requirements or acceptance criteria
    - The approach or implementation strategy
    - Dependencies or assumptions
    - Anything unclear in the task description

    **Ask them now.** Raise any concerns before starting work.

    ## Your Job

    Once you're clear on requirements:
    1. Implement exactly what the task specifies
    2. Write tests (following TDD if task says to)
    3. Verify implementation works
    4. Commit your work
    5. Self-review (see below)
    6. Report back

    Work from: [directory]

    **While you work:** If you encounter something unexpected or unclear, **ask questions**.
    It's always OK to pause and clarify. Don't guess or make assumptions.

    While iterating, run the focused test for what you're changing; run the
    full suite once before committing, not after every edit.

    ## Code Organization

    You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more
    reliable when files are focused. Keep this in mind:
    - Follow the file structure defined in the plan
    - Each file should have one clear responsibility with a well-defined interface
    - If a file you're creating is growing beyond the plan's intent, stop and report
      it as DONE_WITH_CONCERNS — don't split files on your own without plan guidance
    - If an existing file you're modifying is already large or tangled, work carefully
      and note it as a concern in your report
    - In existing codebases, follow established patterns. Improve code you're touching
      the way a good developer would, but don't restructure things outside your task.

    ## When You're in Over Your Head

    It is always OK to stop and say "this is too hard for me." Bad work is worse than
    no work. You will not be penalized for escalating.

    **STOP and escalate when:**
    - The task requires architectural decisions with multiple valid approaches
    - You need to understand code beyond what was provided and can't find clarity
    - You feel uncertain about whether your approach is correct
    - The task involves restructuring existing code in ways the plan didn't anticipate
    - You've been reading file after file trying to understand the system without progress

    **How to escalate:** Report back with status BLOCKED or NEEDS_CONTEXT. Describe
    specifically what you're stuck on, what you've tried, and what kind of help you need.
    The controller can provide more context, re-dispatch with a more capable model,
    or break the task into smaller pieces.

    ## Before Reporting Back: Self-Review

    Review your work with fresh eyes. Ask yourself:

    **Completeness:**
    - Did I fully implement everything in the spec?
    - Did I miss any requirements?
    - Are there edge cases I didn't handle?

    **Quality:**
    - Is this my best work?
    - Are names clear and accurate (match what things do, not how they work)?
    - Is the code clean and maintainable?

    **Discipline:**
    - Did I avoid overbuilding (YAGNI)?
    - Did I only build what was requested?
    - Did I follow existing patterns in the codebase?

    **Testing:**
    - Do tests actually verify behavior (not just mock behavior)?
    - Did I follow TDD if required?
    - Are tests comprehensive?
    - Is the test output pristine (no stray warnings or noise)?

    If you find issues during self-review, fix them now before reporting.

    ## After Review Findings

    If a reviewer finds issues and you fix them, re-run the tests that cover
    the amended code and append the results to your report file. Reviewers
    will not re-run tests for you — your report is the test evidence.

    ## Report Format

    Write your full report to [REPORT_FILE]:
    - What you implemented (or what you attempted, if blocked)
    - What you tested and test results
    - **TDD Evidence** (if TDD was required for this task):
      - RED: command run, relevant failing output before implementation, and why the failure was expected
      - GREEN: command run and relevant passing output after implementation
    - Files changed
    - Self-review findings (if any)
    - Any issues or concerns

    Then report back with ONLY (under 15 lines — the detail lives in the
    report file):
    - **Status:** DONE | DONE_WITH_CONCERNS | BLOCKED | NEEDS_CONTEXT
    - Commits created (short SHA + subject)
    - One-line test summary (e.g. "14/14 passing, output pristine")
    - Your concerns, if any
    - The report file path

    If BLOCKED or NEEDS_CONTEXT, put the specifics in the final message
    itself — the controller acts on it directly.

    Use DONE_WITH_CONCERNS if you completed the work but have doubts about correctness.
    Use BLOCKED if you cannot complete the task. Use NEEDS_CONTEXT if you need
    information that wasn't provided. Never silently produce work you're unsure about.
```
